frameworks.name: Four Levers for Supply Constraint Resolution
frameworks.definition: Four operational decisions (price, delivery ratio, productization, hiring) can resolve capacity constraints; the choice depends on team bandwidth and which lever is most efficient to pull first.

claims.text: When a business has two overlapping front-end offers (e.g., 7.5K for 28 days and 2.8K for 7 days), the lower-priced offer functions as a downsell rather than an upsell, creating operational overlap and preventing clean customer segmentation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: two front-end offers with overlapping audience
lower offer converts from same traffic source

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's poker coaching business is demand-constrained on the higher-ticket offer (7.5K for 28 days, ~12 sales/month) rather than supply-constrained, because the limiting factor is conversion and lead generation, not delivery capacity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The core operational bottleneck for this poker coaching business is not delivery or pricing, but the ability to sell more customers into the front-end offer because the founder is the primary salesperson and is simultaneously constrained by coaching delivery.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The founder cannot simultaneously coach (limiting delivery) and sell (limiting top-of-funnel), creating a binding constraint on overall sales volume.

claims.text: Before cutting either the low-ticket or high-ticket offer, a business should first reconfigure operations to increase delivery capacity by 3-5x, because cutting either offer while demand-generation is weak results in revenue loss rather than optimization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid demand generation not yet enabled
claims.mechanism: If either offer is cut before scaling delivery, you lose sales without the ability to fill the funnel via paid acquisition, eroding overall revenue.
bounded_by: Does not apply if paid demand generation is already running and delivering consistent volume

claims.text: The recommended sequence to scale a service business with overlapping offers is: (1) Fix operations to increase delivery capacity, (2) Activate paid demand generation, (3) Then decide which offer to emphasize or cut based on capacity and margin preference.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Assumes organic demand is currently sufficient; does not apply to businesses with insufficient initial demand

claims.text: A Veblen good effect may apply to premium service offerings: higher pricing can increase credibility and belief in the offer's value, particularly with buyers who use price as a quality signal (e.g., poker players or gamblers).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: avatar uses price as quality signal
service is perceived as luxury or high-status
claims.mechanism: Buyers in status-conscious or risk-aware niches interpret low pricing as a red flag (appears too cheap to be legitimate), whereas higher pricing signals confidence and results.
bounded_by: Does not apply to price-sensitive mass markets
Does not apply to service buyers who actively distrust premium pricing

claims.text: Before raising prices on a service offer, conduct pricing research to determine whether the current price is below market-clearing level, because in one case Hormozi doubled a price and conversion rate actually increased due to the original underpricing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: acquiring the business or revising pricing
claims.mechanism: Low prices sometimes reduce perceived value and buyer belief in the offer; raising price to market-clearing level can increase conversion if price was the bottleneck, not demand.

claims.text: When a business has insufficient demand-generation infrastructure (e.g., organic inbound only), cutting a lower-ticket offer loses revenue without improving margins because paid acquisition is not yet enabled to replace lost volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business relies on organic or warm inbound only
no paid acquisition channel currently running
bounded_by: Does not apply if paid demand generation is already running and can replace lost offer volume

claims.text: A service business can only make smart offer-simplification decisions (cutting the low-ticket offer to focus on high-ticket) once it has both sufficient delivery capacity and working paid demand-generation channels to ensure offer cuts do not reduce overall volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: two overlapping offers with different price points

examples.text: Hormozi's team acquired a business that was significantly underpriced. After conducting pricing research, they identified that the true market price was 2x the current offer price. It took nine conversations with the founder to build conviction around the price increase, but once implemented, not only did close rate increase (because the low price had signaled low quality), but margin improved dramatically. This example illustrates how pricing research can uncover value capture opportunities that simultaneously improve conversion.

The poker coaching business in the transcript has 12 sales/month of the 7.5K offer and 16-32 sales/month of the 2.8K offer (on wide range suggests inconsistent volume). The high-ticket offer requires the founder to personally deliver coaching bootcamps, while the low-ticket offer has lower delivery requirements per transaction, enabling higher volume. This creates operational overlap: the founder is both the primary salesperson and the primary coach, preventing him from scaling either offer independently.

The poker coaching founder originally contemplated cutting the low-ticket offer to focus entirely on the high-ticket 7.5K offer. However, Hormozi identified that this move would immediately lose revenue because the business does not yet have paid demand-generation capability. The business is currently dependent on warm inbound from content marketing, which is growing slowly. If the lower offer is cut, the warm inbound traffic still exists but now has nowhere to convert, resulting in lost revenue with no offsetting paid acquisition to replace it.

practices.text: Before deciding to cut a lower-priced offer in a multi-offer model, first build delivery capacity (3-5x improvement) and activate paid demand generation, then re-evaluate offer strategy.
When scaling a service business with multiple price points, prioritize operational improvements (delivery efficiency) before making pricing or offer decisions.
Conduct pricing research before raising prices on a service offer to determine true market-clearing level and avoid leaving value on the table.
For niche audiences that use price as a quality signal (e.g., gamblers, status-conscious buyers), test higher pricing before accepting current price as optimal.
